articles.title: Animal rights activist attacks NYC horse carriage driver with skateboard during tirade, union says
articles.summary: Abigail Holbrook allegedly punched two Central Park horse carriage drivers and struck one with a skateboard after screaming about animal abuse.
articles.body: An angry animal rights activist armed with a skateboard allegedly assaulted two horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park on Tuesday after launching an expletive-laden tirade in front of visiting families, union representatives said. Abigail Holbrook, 27, of Philadelphia, was arrested after screaming at drivers and accusing them of "animal abuse" near a carriage stand, according to police and video of the incident. "You’re animal abusers! Horses do not do well in New York City. They are very sensitive to light and noise," Holbrook shouted, according to video of the confrontation. "The people that are f------ using these horses are animal abusers. I’m Squid the Kid, bro. Y’all will know my f------ name." MAMDANI ACCUSED OF BETRAYING NYC WORKERS AS UNION BOSS BLASTS 'ANTI-LABOR' HORSE CARRIAGE BAN During the altercation, Holbrook punched two 45-year-old drivers and struck one of them in the head with her skateboard, the Transport Workers Union of America (TWU) told Fox News Digital. Both victims suffered minor injuries and declined medical treatment at the scene. Holbrook was taken into custody by the New York City Police Department and is charged with two counts of assault. VIGIL PLANNED FOR 18-YEAR-OLD TOURIST KILLED IN CENTRAL PARK HORSE-DRAWN CARRIAGE INCIDENT "This is outrageous and unacceptable," TWU Local 100 Administrative Vice President Alexander Kemp said in a statement. "We need a more visible police presence for our members at horse-carriage stands in the park to protect against these wackos. This is their place of work and people are coming just to harass and attack them. All workers deserve to be safe at work." Christina Hansen, a union shop steward who witnessed the assault and alerted police, placed the blame on rhetoric from city leadership and advocacy groups. MAN KILLED AFTER HORSE-DRAWN CARRIAGE BOLTS AND FLIPS NEAR POPULAR NEW YORK CITY TOURIST DESTINATION "The problem is that a lot of people, you know, don't know anything about horses, and they get misled by these animal rights groups who liken it to slavery, and say that the horses are being tortured by being forced to drag heavy carriages around as if carriages don't have wheels," Hansen told Fox News Digital. Hansen noted that the financial livelihoods of carriage drivers depend on whether their horses are well taken care of. "Let's face it, these organizations ... make money by getting donations and there's no money to be made by telling people that our horses are well taken care of," she said. "I only make money if my horse is well taken care of because I can't go to work if he can't pull the carriage, if he doesn't enjoy his job ... so my monetary interest is that my horse is taken care of. Their monetary interest is that the horses are being abused or exploited or whatever." The violence erupted amid ongoing legal and political battles surrounding the city's historic carriage industry. CLASH IN THE CASTLE: MEDIEVAL TIMES DINNER THEATER INSIDERS ALLEGE ANIMAL CRUELTY, SEXUAL HARASSMENT Last month, the city council voted 40 to 7 to pass Romanch's Law, named in memory of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who died in June after being thrown from a runaway carriage in Central Park. The legislation would phase out horse-drawn carriages entirely by June 1, 2028, while directing the city to establish a transition program for more than 150 drivers and industry workers. In a statement to Fox News Digital, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) pushed back against the union's accusations. "If the horse-drawn carriage trade is suddenly concerned about hostility and violence, it might start by looking in the mirror," the group said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Horse-drawn carriages have been a staple of Central Park and Fifth Avenue for generations, providing iconic rides for tourists visiting the city. "Carriage horses have been pulling carriages in Central Park since the day the park opened in December 1858," said Hansen. "They've been living on Manhattan since 1625. The city would not be the city that it is, and Central Park would not be the park that it is, except for horses."

articles.title: Kirk Herbstreit serving steak to his dog at an NYC restaurant has Craig Carton fuming mad
articles.summary: Kirk Herbstreit fed his golden retriever Peter a steak at an NYC steakhouse, sparking a heated debate over dogs in restaurants and food safety rules.
articles.body: Has Kirk Herbstreit taken his dog content too far? On Thursday, Herbstreit's content team bragged across multiple social media channels that Kirk's golden retriever, Peter, "got into another steak in NYC last night," even though it was the football analyst who cut up the steak like he was about to serve it to a six-year-old child. Go ahead, dog lovers, yell at me: joe.kinsey@outkick.com "I wish he would enjoy it," Herbstreit, or one of his sons, wrote on social media after the dog ate the steak off a plate on the floor of the unidentified restaurant in 30 seconds. Of course the entire scene was recorded because why take the dog to an NYC steakhouse if you're not going to turn it into fresh content for the Internet to gorge on. Dog lovers tell OutKick that a dog eating steak off a plate laid on the floor of a high-end NYC steakhouse is not only no big deal, but that it should be the norm. TRAVELERS CLASH OVER WHETHER CRUISE LINES SHOULD ALLOW DOGS AND CATS ON BOARD OR NOT "Love Peter. One time I couldn’t eat all my bacon and I shared it with someone else’s dog I didn’t even know at a restaurant. I love it when I see dogs anywhere. Grocery shopping. Airplanes. Restaurants," dog love Linsey Speech told us on Facebook. Does Kirk need an intervention? We're talking about an NYC steakhouse. "Did he hurt anyone by doing that? Sounds like a judgmental busy body looking to disparage someone," some guy named Kent fired back. OutKick's Craig Carton has a message for Herbstreit over his steakhouse antics "I'm not anti-dog. I just don't want to go to a steakhouse and eat next to a dog. Because it's disgusting," Carton said on Friday while noting that Kirk had to document the whole scene because content is content and Kirk has to constantly feed the algorithm. RESTAURANT OWNER SAYS DINING ROOM IS 'NOT A PLAYGROUND' AS ETIQUETTE EXPERTS WEIGH IN ON VIRAL DEBATE "Now you're sharing your meal with A DOG," Craig continued. "That's right, now the dog is eating on the floor next to you because Kirk Herbstreit doesn't care about your opportunity to enjoy yourself. And have a nice steak meal. He's more concerned that his dog gets to have steak." Meanwhile, the dog truthers are adamant that people like Carton need to stop picking on Kirk. "This is a stupid post….Do you not have anything better to do or say. A lot of people who love animals, are enjoying these posts….why don’t you go elsewhere with your negativity," Roger Graham told OutKick. The "pro-dogs eating in restaurants" community is absolutely furious with OutKick for having the audacity to question Herbstreit's dining habits with his dog. "Or......or........hear me out....How about you mind your own business. What and where he lets his dog eat is none of your concern as long as he's not harming anyone else. Try it once. Minding your own business is good for your health. Farming for clicks," dog lover Mike Lemke lectured. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! According to the FDA, "under federal food safety guidelines and state health codes, standard companion pets are banned from indoor dining rooms." Federal laws also ban emotional support animals from inside restaurants. The dog lovers, who have spent Friday yelling at OutKick about how dogs should be permitted to eat their hearts out at steakhouses, need to know that even under the Americans with Disabilities Act, service dogs aren't permitted to use dishes designated for human customers. But, they just keep yelling at us that Herbstreit's dog should be allowed to do what he wants. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER "OMG! This is a HUGE stretch for content. I watched the video, and his dog is so well-behaved and deserves all the steak. DARN it! I just fed into this algorithm grab," Barb complained. Rules are rules, Barb.

articles.title: Everyone accounted for after tanker collides with a New Orleans riverboat
articles.summary: A large tanker ship struck a riverboat with more than 100 passengers in New Orleans on Friday, capsizing the cruise vessel and prompting a major rescue effort in the Mississippi River.
articles.body: A large tanker ship struck a riverboat with more than 100 passengers in New Orleans on Friday, capsizing the cruise vessel and prompting a major rescue effort in the Mississippi River. The American Heritage ship, managed by American Cruise Lines, was T-boned by the tanker while docked near the French Quarter, a spokesperson said in a statement. Thirty-two passengers were hospitalized in the collision, though none of those injuries were critical, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told reporters. All of the passengers had been accounted for, she said. Moreno called that fact “a miracle on the Mississippi.” The cause of the crash was unclear and remained under investigation, Moreno said. The U.S. Coast Guard and National Transportation Safety Board will conduct that investigation. The transportation officials were delayed in making their way to the Crescent City because of the ground stop at airports across the nation, officials said. There were nearly 130 passengers on board the Heritage, which had been docked in the port for about two hours before the incident, NBC affiliate WDSU reported. Officials said the tanker lost control and collided with the riverboat at 12:30 p.m. in the Port of New Orleans, one of the nation’s largest ports. While passengers were disembarking, the riverboat began to sink and flipped, Moreno said. “When that occurred, we started to have people in the water,” she said. She described the effort to rescue those passengers as an “all hands on deck approach.” The American Heritage, which had been set to embark on a seven-day cruise to Mississippi, eventually capsized. Video and images verified by NBC News show a number of people wearing life jackets in the water near the site of the crash. A passenger who was on the riverboat told NBC News that she had to crawl to safety after the collision. “After the initial crash, it hit us again and we flipped over and I had to crawl over the railing and people to save myself,” Rhonda Akers said. Akers said her husband was hospitalized with a head injury and she was waiting to see him. A 3-mile stretch of the river was closed to traffic while responders assessed the situation. A Coast Guard official told reporters that authorities were working to reopen the waterway as soon as possible. Atlantic Asphalt, the tanker that struck the cruise vessel, is based in the Marshall Islands and is owned by Chinese and Liberian companies, according to public records.

articles.title: Pakistan 80 years old, can't appropriate Indus Valley civilisation: Culture minister
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Culture minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat Friday expressed hope that Pakistan will participate in the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Culture minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat Friday expressed hope that Pakistan will participate in the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in Delhi from Nov 20 to 22, even as he trashed Pakistan's attempts to appropriate Indus Valley civilisation, pointing out that the neighbouring nation came into existence only around 80 years ago.Fifteen countries, including China, Iran, UAE, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, have confirmed their participation for the event, which India will host at the historic Purana Quila complex. Pakistan is yet to respond to the invite. PM Narendra Modi will attend the inaugural ceremony of the dialogue forum, where India will showcase its 5,000-year-old civilisational journey.Shekhawat highlighted that PM had proposed the establishment of a Civilisational Dialogue Forum at the 2025 SCO Summit in Tianjin, and it was subsequently, welcomed and endorsed, with India announcing to host the inaugural forum.The invitation to Pakistan gains significance as it happens to be the first New Delhi has extended after Operation Sindoor last year. Ministers of 25 countries were invited, of which 15 countries have confirmed participation so far, he added.When asked about attempts by a "neighbouring country" to appropriate Indus Valley civilisation, he said if a country is trying to make such a claim, the question to ask is that "did they even exist then". "They (Pakistan) came into existence only around 80 years ago..." he said.The minister noted that Pakistan's civilisational and cultural evolution is no different from India as the former became a separate country after Partition in 1947. "So, at least on this aspect there should be no space for differences... Moreover, whatever may be a country's geopolitical, strategic and bilateral ties, one must take a step forward to reinforce cultural relations so that it can help build better dialogue and coordination between people of the two countries," he said.The minister said Purana Qila provides an appropriate setting for the forum as the archaeological excavations at the site have revealed cultural layers and evidence of early settlements dating back to approximately 1200 BCE.The four broad themes of the dialogue are civilisational and cultural expressions; art and architecture; language, literature, script and manuscript traditions; and monastic trails.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption
articles.summary: Experts say the event is a "stark reminder" of how heavily the world relies on a small group of big tech providers.
articles.body:
Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.

Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.

The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.

Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.

Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.

Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.

By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.

Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?

Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world

UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.

In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.

In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.

Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.

In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.

The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.

Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business was basically brought to a "standstill".

His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" was been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".

Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she was due to complete her first house purchase today after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that.

"The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies.

"We're not the only one completing today, there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible," Georgia said.

Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.

While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.

By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.

Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remain stable once they are up and running again.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.

"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."

Microsoft said it has no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered.

A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.

Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.

"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.

Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.

"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said .

"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

articles.title: Ground stop ordered for all airports nationwide for ‘reasons of safety’
articles.summary: Much of the air traffic across the U.S. was shut down suddenly Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for all departing flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
articles.body: Much of the air traffic across the U.S. was shut down suddenly Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for all departing flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” The unusual alert, which was issued at 3:54 p.m. ET, contained no other information beyond stating that “all departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.” Follow along for live coverage. “Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis,” the FAA said. When the FAA issued the alert, 4,042 flights destined for US airports were airborne, according to Flightradar24, a Swedish service that displays real-time aircraft flight tracking information. By 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, was at capacity, and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, meaning there was no place for the planes to park, a source with knowledge told NBC News. With planes stranded on runway, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was “no indication as of yet” that there was anything “nefarious” that caused the ground stop. He said it was the result of a telecommunications outage “as of now.” Mullin said President Donald Trump has been briefed and they are “are not ruling out anything at this point” in terms of what caused the communications issue. He said those currently on flights have no reason for concern. “We are assured that everybody is safe,” he said, adding that it was unprecedented. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in an online post. “We will provide immediate updates as we have them.” Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti called the outage “extraordinary” and said he doesn’t know what would cause it. Guzzetti emphasized that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing. He added that the situation is moving from a safety issue to instead becoming a massive logistics problem. Airports could quickly become crowded with planes trying to land as the aircraft currently on the ground aren’t able to depart. Planes on the ground may have to move and park on taxiways, Guzzetti said. There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and then the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are affected by the outage. Shortly before the FAA issued its alert, both major airports in Chicago — O’Hare and Midway International Airport — were listed on a ground stop alert due to an “equipment outage,” NBC Chicago reported. Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded. “At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’” Werne, a consultant who helps manufacturers and other industries adapt AI technology, said he is a frequent flyer and this was a first for him. He said there was “a mixture of emotions” from his fellow passengers on hearing the announcement. “Then I started hearing from other friends who were on planes, including one in Chicago who was stuck on a runway,” Werne said. “Right now, our plane is heading back to the terminal, so at least we’re going to be able to deplane.” At Newark Liberty International Airport, personnel in the control tower said the situation is “a whole mess right now,” according to LiveATC. “We’re running out of space” and “there’s significant gate issues” were comments also heard on the live audio feed. “I’m as much in the dark as everyone else. I’m not getting any information from anybody,” one controller at Newark said, according to the feed. United Airlines issued a statement acknowledging the ground stop. “United flights that are already airborne will continue,” the statement said. “New domestic flights will not depart while the FAA ground stop remains in place.” Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare. After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports. In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.

articles.title: Teens raised by strict, obey-without-question parents tend to hold more antisocial beliefs, a US study found, and they also showed small rises in anxiety and depression
articles.summary: \"Because I said so\" is probably one of the most frequently heard lines in a strict household.
articles.body: "Because I said so" is probably one of the most frequently heard lines in a strict household. For some parents, discipline means setting rules and expecting their children to follow them blindly, without questioning or challenging their decisions.Many parents believe they have unquestionable authority over their children, almost a sense of ownership, simply because they brought them into the world. "I kept you, I carried you for nine months" is something many children might have heard while growing up. But how often do parents stop to consider whether their children ever asked to be born? They did not ask their parents to bring them into the world. Having children was the parents' decision, and that decision came with the responsibility of raising another individual, not owning one. Children do not owe their parents their individuality or unquestioning obedience. If anything, parents owe their children the freedom to grow into individuals of their own.The times become especially tough when the child matures a little and develops a sense of individuality, a personality of their own. For the first time in their lives, they begin to think of themselves as separate from their parents, and probably that is why adolescence is the hardest time for parents. This is the time when the real test of a parent-child relationship happens. Either, after adolescence, the child comes out as their parents' best friend or becomes a stranger connected by the surname. People who are strict as parents think they are doing their child a favour, keeping them safe and disciplined or getting them ready for the real world. But do you know this might be affecting the psyche of their children more than they even realise? A new US study suggests that teenagers raised by authoritarian parents, who place a strong emphasis on obedience and unquestioning compliance, tend to hold more antisocial beliefs.A study titled "Longitudinal associations between authoritarian parenting and adolescent antisocial thinking, depression, and anxiety: Between- and within-person effects", led by researchers Wusirige and Bo Jian, along with Gabriel J. Merrin, examined how authoritarian parenting practices are associated with teenagers' antisocial thinking and mental health.Published in the Journal of Research on Adolescence, the study followed 491 US adolescents, with an average age of 15.28 years, across four waves of data collection between November 2021 and summer 2023. The researchers examined whether parenting practices characterised by strict control, hostility and punishment were associated with changes in adolescents' antisocial beliefs, anxiety and depressive symptoms over time.Teenagers with authoritarian parents showed more antisocial thinkingAccording to the US National Institutes of Health (NIH), antisocial behaviour involves a persistent disregard for other people's rights and social norms. It can include behaviours such as deceitfulness, impulsivity, aggression, irritability and a lack of remorse for actions that cause harm. Sounds horrible, doesn't it? But antisocial tendencies do not always begin with such extreme behaviour. They can also take shape through the attitudes and beliefs a person develops towards others, including a tendency to justify aggression, disregard rules or show little concern for how their actions affect other people. During adolescence, these beliefs are still developing and can influence how young people understand and respond to the world around them.The researchers examined how authoritarian parenting was associated with teenagers' attitudes towards antisocial behaviour. They found that adolescents who experienced higher levels of authoritarian parenting tended to show more persistent antisocial thinking over time. This included beliefs that could justify behaviours such as bullying others or breaking rules. In other words, teenagers who experienced stricter, more controlling parenting were also more likely to hold attitudes that normalised harmful or disruptive behaviour.Authoritarian parenting was also linked to anxiety and depression in teenagersApart from antisocial thinking, the researchers also examined whether authoritarian parenting had any association with anxiety and depression among teenagers. They found that the relationship was not as straightforward. While higher levels of authoritarian parenting were not significantly associated with higher anxiety and depression across the group as a whole, the researchers did observe an increase in these symptoms among individual teenagers over time. This association became apparent at the final stage of the study, around 18 months after the initial assessment.The researchers, however, caution against considering authoritarian parenting the sole cause of antisocial behaviour among teenagers. The study does establish an association between the two, which cannot be ignored.Parenting is not simply about teaching children what to do and what not to do. It is also about helping them understand why certain choices matter and allowing them the space to make decisions, question ideas and develop their own judgement. Rules and discipline have their place, but when obedience becomes more important than understanding, the relationship between parents and children can suffer. After all, the purpose of raising a child should not be to create someone who follows every instruction without question, but an individual who can think independently, respect others and make sense of the world on their own.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Ohio bank foreclosed on a home while its owner was in prison for murdering his wife; after the property sold with $61,060 left over, a November 10 appeals court revived his challenge over how the papers were served
articles.summary: A foreclosure case that appeared to be over is back in court after an Ohio appeals court raised questions about whether the property owner had been
articles.body: A foreclosure case that appeared to be over is back in court after an Ohio appeals court raised questions about whether the property owner had been properly notified of the original proceedings. The homeowner, who is serving time for the murder of his wife, lost his Columbus home to a foreclosure initiated by the bank while he was behind bars. But the case resurfaced when a separate dispute erupted over who would get the money after the sheriff's sale produced more than $61,000 in surplus proceeds. The Tenth District Court of Appeals in Ohio on Nov. 10, 2026, reversed a lower court’s denial of a motion to reconsider a foreclosure judgment. The court ruled that the owner's later participation in the proceedings could not be grounds for an automatic finding that he had been properly served in the course of the proceedings.Bank moves forward with foreclosure while homeowner is in jailThe property, located at Noe Bixby Road in Columbus, belonged to Mamadou Diallo, according to the Ohio Court of Appeals, Tenth District. He entered into a mortgage with JPMorgan Chase Bank in October 2017.Nationstar Mortgage LLC sued Diallo in May 2023 for mortgage default and foreclosure. US Bank Trust National Association later substituted Nationstar as the plaintiff and filed an amended foreclosure complaint in June 2024. At the time, Diallo was incarcerated at Southeastern Correctional Institution. Court documents show that a first attempt to serve him by certified mail was unsuccessful. A process server later testified that he served the prison’s intake officer with the summons and complaint in August 2024. The court docket also shows certified mail delivery to the institution.Property sold for over $61,000 in surplus fundsThe Ohio Court of Appeals, Tenth District, said the bank filed a request for a default judgment, which the Franklin County court granted and issued a foreclosure decree on Oct. 21, 2024.The property was then sold at sheriff’s auction on April 25, 2025. After the sale, the relevant obligations were paid and there were excess proceeds of $61,060.07.In October 2025, Diallo asked that the surplus be distributed. But the estate of his late wife also filed a request for the money. But the appeals court said Diallo’s claim was dismissed by the magistrate because he was convicted of murdering his wife, Fatoumata Diallo, who died in September 2021. Ohio’s slayer statute prohibits a person convicted of killing another from profiting from the victim’s death. The court therefore awarded the entire surplus to his wife’s estate.Homeowner behind bars challenges his serviceRecords from the Ohio Court of Appeals, Tenth District, show Diallo later challenged the foreclosure judgment, saying he never personally received the summons or complaint.He argued the service process was defective and had not been completed within the time limits imposed by Ohio Civil Rule 3(A). He also testified that he did not become aware of the foreclosure proceedings or the sheriff's sale until September 15, 2025. In May 2026, a lower court refused to vacate the judgment. By participating in subsequent proceedings regarding the surplus funds without raising any service concerns, he had waived his objection.Timing is important, appeals court saysIn its Nov. 10 ruling, the Ohio Court of Appeals, Tenth District, did not agree with the lower court’s reasoning.Before a court can render a judgment that is binding on the parties, the court must first establish personal jurisdiction over the defendant, the appellate judges said. This can be done by proper service, voluntary submission to jurisdiction before judgment or other conduct evidencing submission to the authority of the court.But the timing of such participation is important. Any post-judgment acts that might have been invalid cannot retroactively cure a jurisdictional defect, the appellate court held. Because Diallo's efforts to claim the surplus were made months after the foreclosure decree, they could not automatically operate as a waiver of his earlier objection to service.Case returned for further actionThe Tenth District Court of Appeals in Ohio reversed the lower court’s ruling and sent the case back to Franklin County for further proceedings.The appeals court, crucially, did not void the bank's service or nullify the foreclosure. Instead, the court told the lower court to consider whether Diallo had been properly served or had otherwise submitted to its jurisdiction before the foreclosure judgment was entered. The appellate court likewise refused to address his distinct claim that he was denied a hearing, because the reversal rendered that issue unnecessary to decide.The November 10 ruling doesn’t address the key question of whether service was proper, sending the case back to the trial court for further proceedings.Images Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: New campaign against EU membership launches ahead of UK-EU summit
articles.summary: The launch of Stay Out comes as Andy Burnham prepares for talks with European leaders next week.
articles.body:
A new campaign against the UK rejoining the European Union has been launched ahead of a UK-EU summit next week.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility on 20 November, arguing a "win-win" deal can be struck .

But Stay Out has warned any future attempt to rejoin the EU could prove costly to taxpayers and the UK should "move on and spend our money on our own priorities".

The group has received support from Lord Gove, chairman of the Vote Leave campaign during the 2016 EU referendum, who warned reopening the Brexit question would "commit the country to another decade of fractious negotiations".

He said: "Rejoining would mean handing back control of our laws, borders, money and trade, and paying a good deal more for membership than we did before."

He added people are "desperate for Westminster to get on with delivering on their priorities" rather than looking to rejoin the EU.

Stay Out is chaired by Oliver Lewis, who also worked for Vote Leave, and acted as deputy chief negotiator for the UK government in trade negotiations with the bloc.

Lewis said: "The country has had enough of arguing about Europe, and it is time to move on and spend our money on our own priorities."

Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others

Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham

The campaign's launch has been accompanied by analysis from the group which claims rejoining the EU would cost the UK £39.3bn a year in contributions, or £750m a week.

BBC News has not independently verified the group's calculations.

Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good" but has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election.

He has said he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.

In September, Burnham was asked if he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU. He replied that he wanted to "look at the options".

The prime minister added that he had previously advocated such a move within his lifetime, whilst acknowledging it was "not necessarily the case that that is now".

articles.title: Meet Gus Fandrich, the Martensville, Saskatchewan boy who was 10 when he built an ice cream-selling bike with his father and served up to 100 customers some days
articles.summary: Gus Fandrich of Gus’ Sweet Treats, a young entrepreneur from Martensville, Saskatchewan, was 10 years old when he started selling ice cream from a bike
articles.body: Gus Fandrich of Gus’ Sweet Treats, a young entrepreneur from Martensville, Saskatchewan, was 10 years old when he started selling ice cream from a bike that he built with help from his father. As of June 2026, the mobile ice cream business travels all around town on Fridays and weekends, and on some days it serves up to 100 people. His father explained that such bikes used to sell ice cream, and Gus asked whether he could do the same. His father told him he could. Jason Fandrich said Gus simply wanted to do something and has always been motivated, so the family pulled the project together for him.Inside the ice cream bike, a freezer, an inverter and an electric motor were built with his fatherWith help from his father, Gus built the bike himself. Jason Fandrich said they decided to go the route of a freezer and an inverter. Gus then wanted to sell pop and chips as well, so the pair added a small compartment to the back. They also fitted an electric motor and an e-bike throttle, completing the setup that carries the business around town.Gus said the business has let him learn more about his city and meet new people from across town. articles.title: 87-year-old disabled California wildfire survivor says contractor went $90K over budget, wants another $51K; claims dispute has left him homeless and broke after losing Eaton Fire home
articles.summary: An 87-year-old disabled California wildfire survivor says a dispute with a contractor rebuilding his home has left him homeless and financially drained,
articles.body: An 87-year-old disabled California wildfire survivor says a dispute with a contractor rebuilding his home has left him homeless and financially drained, months after losing his house in the devastating Eaton Fire. Peter Brown, an Army veteran from Altadena, Los Angeles County, claims he has paid hundreds of thousands of dollars towards rebuilding his wheelchair-accessible home, only to be told that he needs to pay another $51,000 to get the project completed.Brown lost his home in the 2025 Eaton Fire, one of two major wildfires that devastated parts of Los Angeles County and displaced an estimated 205,000 people in Altadena and Pacific Palisades. Hoping to return to a safe and accessible home, he hired modular home building company Menu Homes to construct a replacement within a year.According to Brown, he paid the company $538,000 for the project but eventually had to shell out another $90,000 in additional costs. Despite the extra payment, he says the contractor is now demanding another $51,000 to finish the house."I've run out of money. He's drained me. I just don't have the $51,000," Brown told CBS News. "He's just taking everything. And that was going to be my savings."87-year-old says he has run out of insurance money and is paying rentWith the agreed completion deadline having passed and the house still unfinished, Brown says he has exhausted his insurance funds as well. He is currently paying $2,500 a month in rent while waiting to return to his home.The prolonged rebuilding process has left him struggling to meet basic living expenses. A GoFundMe campaign has been launched to support the Army veteran, explaining that he "needs our help with basic living expenses and the remaining costs of getting back into his home."For Brown, the situation has become particularly difficult because the new property was supposed to provide the wheelchair accessibility he needs. Instead, he remains without a permanent home and says he has no savings left to meet the contractor's latest demand.Contractor blames county permitting delays; town council members question explanationMenu Homes has offered a different explanation for the delay. Bobby Shokri, a representative of the company, attributed the holdups to Los Angeles County requirements and months of permitting approvals. He also said additional features, including a garage and porch, expanded the scope of the project."We had a contract for a certain scope of work — the county imposed additional scope of work," Shokri said.However, some Altadena Town Council members have questioned the contractor's explanation. Morgan Whirledge acknowledged that the county's permitting process had not been perfect, given the huge number of rebuilding projects following the fires. However, he said officials had streamlined what was previously a notoriously bureaucratic process and waived all permit fees."Many of the delays are due to contractors or professionals who may be taking a long time responding to comments from the county," Whirledge told Moneywise.He also questioned the additional charges allegedly being passed on to Brown, arguing that they should not fall on a homeowner with limited resources who had already agreed to a contract price. Whirledge pointed to Contractors State License Board guidance for disaster rebuilding, which he said states that contracts must be fixed-price.Another council member, Darlene Green, told CBS News that homeowners should not be caught off guard by changes to a rebuilding project."If something changes, it shouldn't be a shock. And it certainly shouldn't be hundreds of thousands of dollars over the initial asking," she said.The dispute remains unresolved.California wildfire survivor's struggle highlights rising cost of disaster recoveryBrown's experience highlights the financial challenges that can continue long after a natural disaster destroys a home. Even when insurance provides some assistance, rebuilding can involve additional expenses, delays and unexpected financial commitments.According to Harvard University's Joint Center for Housing Studies, homeowners across the United States spent approximately $23 billion annually between 2021 and 2023 repairing damage caused by disasters. The average cost per homeowner reached $22,100 in 2023.The financial strain can also build over time. A report by the nonprofit Urban Institute examining the aftermath of Hurricane Helene in 2024 found that survivors sometimes faced growing debt and worsening credit as recovery costs accumulated. For households relying on fixed incomes, these expenses could be particularly difficult to manage. The report also documented a family that cashed out a 401(k) account to stay financially afloat.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Missouri delivery driver pulled into traffic after a trucker waved him through, and a woman's car hit his van; he admitted he could not see the road, and a November 10 appeals court upheld her $800,000 injury award
articles.summary: A Missouri appeals court has upheld an $800,000 jury award for a woman injured when a delivery van pulled into her path after a truck driver waved it
articles.body: A Missouri appeals court has upheld an $800,000 jury award for a woman injured when a delivery van pulled into her path after a truck driver waved it forward. The court found there was no evidence that the woman was driving too fast, and it rejected the defence argument that she shared fault for the crash. The case, Amy Bolandis v. Thomas Bateman and UniFirst Corporation, turned on a simple but important question. Could the driver who pulled out blindly into traffic blame the other motorist for travelling at a normal speed? The Missouri Court of Appeals said no, as per report on Justia U.S. Law. Read more details about it here:What happened on Hall StreetThe crash occurred around 7:05 in the morning on 19 December 2018, on Hall Street in St Louis. Conditions were dry and daylight was clear, with no rain, snow or poor visibility. Thomas Bateman was driving a commercial Freightliner Step Van for UniFirst and was exiting a parking lot. He intended to cross Hall Street, a road with two lanes in each direction plus a centre turn lane.A semitruck had stopped in the right southbound lane to turn into the same parking lot. That truck blocked Bateman’s view to the left and also blocked the view of the oncoming driver, Amy Bolandis, to the right.The wave that changed everythingThe semitruck driver waved Bateman forward, signalling that it was safe to pull out. Bateman did so, and Bolandis’s car struck the rear of his van. Bateman later admitted that the collision was his fault. He said he believed vehicles already on the road had the right of way, but he did not yield to them. He also admitted that he did not check for oncoming traffic or keep a careful lookout. He said he did not see Bolandis’s vehicle until the moment of impact.The injuries and the verdictBolandis suffered a dislocated and broken ankle in the crash. She underwent surgery nine days later and was cleared to return to work in January 2019. Her ankle began hurting again in April 2024, years after the initial injury. An orthopaedic surgeon described the trauma as high velocity, highlighting the severity of the impact.A jury awarded her $800,000 in damages, plus post-judgment interest, as per the report. The defence appealed, arguing that the trial court should have allowed the jury to consider whether Bolandis was driving too fast.The argument over speedThe defence claimed that Bolandis may have been driving at an excessive speed for the conditions, even though she was not over the posted limit. The speed limit on Hall Street was 45 miles per hour, and Bolandis estimated she was travelling around 40 miles per hour.The defence argued that passing other cars, the obstructed view caused by the semitruck and the force of the collision all pointed to excessive speed. They said this should have been left to the jury to decide.The trial court disagreed. It found there was no substantial evidence that Bolandis was driving too fast for the conditions, and it refused to give the jury an instruction on comparative fault.What the appeals court saidThe Missouri Court of Appeals reviewed the case de novo, meaning it looked at the legal question fresh rather than deferring to the trial court. It concluded that the defence had failed to present enough evidence to support a claim of excessive speed.The court noted that Bolandis testified she was driving with the flow of traffic and had passed only a few cars over a four-and-a-half-mile stretch. The defence offered no evidence about the speed of those other cars or the condition of the road.The court also found no evidence that road or visibility conditions required Bolandis to slow down. Without that, the claim that her speed was excessive had no legal basis.Why the wave did not matterOne might assume that the truck driver’s wave would shift some blame away from Bateman. The appeals court did not see it that way.Bateman admitted that he pulled out blindly when his vision was blocked. He also said that if he had seen Bolandis before pulling out, the collision would never have happened.The court held that this admission, combined with the lack of evidence against Bolandis, meant the jury could not reasonably find that her speed contributed to the crash. The wave from the truck driver did not change that conclusion.What this means going forwardThe ruling reinforces a basic principle of road safety. A driver who pulls into traffic must ensure it is safe to do so, regardless of whether another driver signals them forward.It also clarifies that being within the speed limit does not automatically protect a driver from a comparative fault claim. But the defence must show that conditions actually required a slower speed and that the speed prevented the driver from avoiding the crash.For Bolandis, the decision means the $800,000 award stands. For drivers everywhere, it is a reminder that a wave from another motorist is not a substitute for checking the road yourself.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Strengthening rupee may make outbound travel cheaper
articles.summary: Rupee’s rebound to 93.67/USD may lower outbound travel costs for Indians, boosting affordability in dollar-linked destinations despite high airfares.
articles.body: Chennai: Thanks to the rupee staging a rebound against the dollar since late last week and early this week, international travel may now be a tad cheaper and more affordable for people traveling from India, as they will need fewer Indian rupees to purchase US dollars or other foreign currencies tied closely to dollar strength, say travel experts.On Thursday, Nov 12, the rupee gained nearly 6 paise to close at 93.67 against the US dollar - the highest in the last six months - owing to positive domestic markets and foreign inflows.Triggered by the West Asia conflict and global crude oil supply disruptions, Jet fuel prices have been on a rising spree this year. This led to a significant surge in year-end outbound air fares, too. The rupee also hit its lowest point this July, closing at 96.39 per dollar. “With airfares, hotel prices and currency fluctuations putting pressure on travel budgets, people became more conscious of where they spend and how they get the most out of every rupee. Travellers were booking flights and stays much in advance to avoid peak-season price increases and paying closer attention to exchange rates when planning their expenses,” says Taneia Bhardwaj, South Asia expansion lead at cross border payments platform Wise.The recent recovery of the Indian rupee against the US dollar could, however, improve the affordability of international travel, particularly for expenses such as accommodation, shopping, dining and local experiences in destinations whose currencies are closely linked to the dollar, says Rajiv Mehra, general secretary of federation of association of Indian tourism and hospitality (FAITH). “The key trend this year-end is smarter travel planning, with consumers balancing their desire to explore the world against overall value for money,” says Mehra.Agrees Abraham Alapatt, president & group head – marketing of Thomas Cook (India) & SOTC Travel. “The year-end travel period continues to be an important window, and currency movements are an important component of the overall holiday cost,” he says.So, instead of outright cancelling their travel plans, Indians are making flexible itineraries to make the most of the strengthening rupee and get more value on forex. Pavan Kumar Kavad, MD of Prithvi Exchange, says, “Ahead of the year-end holiday season, international airfares had surged by nearly 25% in 2026. But Indian travellers started considering different destinations, modifying their budgets, and adjusting the duration of their trips. We are observing a growing inclination towards Southeast Asian destinations like Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam, over conventional long-haul trips to Europe or West Asia. articles.title: Ruins and restorations: New archive chronicles Scotland's castles
articles.summary: The collection provides a snapshot of the structures and whether or not they are beyond repair.
articles.body:
The global fascination with Scotland's castles shows little sign of dimming.

From Americans fulfilling a lifelong dream to TV star Alan Carr moving into his "turret era", interest in owning one has rarely been higher.

For those of us with more modest budgets, the striking looks and stories behind these structures are an enduring attraction.

Now a new archive hopes to provide a comprehensive, detailed and nationally-accessible picture of the condition of the nation's castles, their history and what their future might hold.

Inside the £3.25m castle bought by Celebrity Traitors winner Alan Carr

Alan Carr bought a Scottish castle. Could you?

Richard Oram has just retired as professor of medieval and environmental history at Stirling University and is president of the Scottish Castles Association (SCA).

He said Dorothy Walker, who previously chaired the group, pushed strongly for the creation of an archive and it is an idea he was happy to run with.

Although there are other collections out there, he said none of them was "as ambitious or as comprehensive" as what they hope theirs can become.

"It's not to be a sort of a closeted-away, academics-and-professionals-only type of thing," he explained.

"This is intended to be nationally-accessible and community-supported.

"It's something that can only really gain its maximum potential by working with other people around the country."

It consists, primarily, of a series of unique images of the buildings which have been built up by a number of people over decades.

"We're either charting the decline from a lived-in building into a ruin or the gradual climbing from being a ruin back into habitation or use," he said.

"A lot of that kind of record doesn't survive in a place that most people can see it.

"They either know the building as a pile of rubble or they know the building as a private house or something of that kind and they don't know how it got from one state into the other."

Among the archive is the Alastair Maxwell-Irving collection of plans and drawings stretching right across the country from Dumfries and Galloway to the North Sea coast.

"I think this is one of the really exciting things for the moment is there's this huge upsurge of interest in Scotland's castles," said Oram.

"It's always been strong, it's always been a recognised part of Scotland's culture and heritage.

"But there's now, once again, this fashion, particularly amongst North Americans, but not just North Americans, for acquiring and living in a romantic Scottish castle and a lot of restoration."

The new collection could help fuel that.

"Amongst the things that we're trying to do with the archive is also produce a body of evidence around what can feasibly be restored and what is actually beyond the point of return," explained Oram.

He said that tied in with Historic Environment Scotland's discussions around "managed decline" and how to allow a building to deteriorate but still be visited if safe and record it appropriately for future generations.

"The goal is something that gives us an up-to-the-minute, sound overview of the building as it is now with a good understanding of its historical development and the history behind that building," he explained.

He said that consisted of telling the story of the people who owned and developed it, but also how it had been adapted over time.

"You've got places that are originally a 14th Century tower, for example, but they've been turned into really comfortable houses in the later 18th, 19th and 20th Centuries," he said.

"So it's what's been compromised, what's been added, what of the original fabric remains."

He said they hoped to "strip away a lot of the mythology" around some buildings and work with communities and organisations around the country to provide the best information possible.

All of it will be available online and also, physically, at Stirling University - and Oram said it would tell the story of the castles as plainly and simply as possible.

"It's to try and get away from some of the really starchy, confined, Secret Squirrel type of language that often descriptions of these buildings are wrapped up in," he said.

A launch of the archive takes place at Dunbar Castle on Wednesday.

"We're trying to really build interest and enthusiasm across the country," he said.

"But I think the critically important thing for us is to really push and get a better understanding of our buildings, our national heritage.

"It's something that we're hopeful will really be there to fire up the enthusiasm of the broader public and all the people that we know around the country that are absolutely passionate about castles."

articles.title: Rescue efforts under way after tanker strikes river cruise boat in US
articles.summary: American Heritage paddleboat with 129 passengers on board is partially submerged on Mississippi River in New Orleans.
articles.body:
A tanker has struck a river cruise boat carrying 129 passengers on the Mississippi River in New Orleans, partially submerging the vessel and prompting a major rescue operation.

The Atlantic Asphalt tanker hit the American Heritage paddleboat on Friday at about 12:30pm local time (18:30 GMT), the Port of New Orleans said. The cruise boat had docked about two hours earlier to begin letting passengers off. The authorities have not released any information on injuries or deaths.

“Multiple individuals have been rescued, and search-and-rescue operations remain ongoing,” a city spokesperson said.

Video from the scene showed the much larger tanker hitting the paddlewheel cruise boat as metal and glass crashed and crunched, according to The Associated Press news agency.

More than a dozen people in life jackets were dragged from the river, where the water temperature was 19 degrees Celsius (66 degrees Fahrenheit), onto nearby ships, while others stood near the railing as the boat listed further into the water.

“Surreal, that’s what that was,” one witness, Jamie Holford, told local television. “Fifteen minutes from impact to where it rolled over.”

Port police, the fire department, the coastguard and emergency medical staff are on the scene, and a triage area was set up inside the port’s administration building. The river was closed to vessel traffic.

American Cruise Lines, which operates the boat, said guests and crew had been evacuated and that it was “deeply concerned for everyone involved”.

The five-deck American Heritage, built in 2015, holds up to 150 passengers and was finishing an eight-day cruise to destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.

The 160-metre (520-foot) tanker was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands and was bound for New Orleans, according to the MarineTraffic tracker. It specialises in carrying asphalt and bitumen, according to the maritime periodical Marine Insights.

The cause of the collision, as well as whether the ship was carrying cargo, remains unknown.

articles.title: FAA ground stop leaves College Football teams stranded on eve of crucial Saturday showdowns
articles.summary: Texas, Tennessee, Utah and other top college football programs were grounded Friday as the FAA ground stop stranded teams before Saturday's games.
articles.body: The FAA ground stop that was issued on Friday afternoon is obviously having an effect on travel across the country, but it's also having a major impact on college football teams scheduled to play on Saturday. The second nationwide ground stop since 9/11 could disrupt travel over the next few days as passengers wait for the FAA to allow flights to resume ahead of a busy travel weekend. But concern is growing across college athletics for teams that have yet to depart for Saturday’s games. MISSISSIPPI STATE’S KAMARIO TAYLOR FINALIZING A REPORTED $7.5 MILLION DEAL, IN WILD COLLEGE FOOTBALL MOVE According to multiple sources, some of those schools who are currently looking for alternative travel include Texas, Tennessee, Ole Miss, Washington, Minnesota, Baylor, Tulane, Auburn, Arizona State, Oregon State and others. USC has already taken off for their trip to Bloomington for a showdown with Indiana, and are currently in the air. For instance, Texas was scheduled to depart Austin and had already boarded its plane for Baton Rouge ahead of Saturday's showdown against LSU, but the FAA had issued the ground stop before they had taken off for Louisiana. In the case of a school like Tennessee, the Vols were scheduled to depart McGee Tyson Airport in Knoxville at 4 p.m. ET, but the FAA notice was issued, and the team was not able to get into the air. How they end up getting to College Station is still to be determined at this moment, though the situation remains fluid. Other schools across the country were lucky under the circumstances, and had already departed for their road game destination. WEEK 8 AP TOP 25 POLL SEES BIG TEN GAIN EQUAL FOOTING ON SEC AND UNBEATEN UTAH EARN MAJOR RESPECT Some schools also had the luxury to take buses to their game, like Alabama traveling to Nashville for its game against Vanderbilt. This could turn out to be the case for a team like Auburn, who is scheduled to play Mississippi State on Saturday in Starkville. But, for No. 2 Utah, the Utes were grounded in Salt Lake City before they were scheduled to take off for their matchup with Arizona on Saturday night. Schools typically travel on Friday afternoons for Saturday games, usually holding a walkthrough at their facility before heading straight to the airport for departure. Also, most schools will have security checkpoints actually set up at their facilities, so they can just get off the bus and board the airplane that is taking them to their destination. articles.title: Woman with terminal cancer has "dream" wedding on Bangor hospital ward
articles.summary: Maggie Heginbothom thanks staff after "dream" ceremony is arranged two days after her partner proposed.
articles.body:
A woman with a terminal cancer diagnosis married her partner of 15 years in the hospital where she is receiving palliative care - and her horses even made the ceremony.

Maggie Heginbothom, 68, who has advanced liver cancer, thanked staff at Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor for organising a wedding ceremony on Monday, just two days after her partner Mark proposed.

The horse lover and former clinical scientist with Public Health Wales described hospital staff as being "like family to me".

"It was so beautiful and I honestly never thought it was going to be possible, especially seeing both my horses there as well," she said.

Heginbothom, originally from the Vale of Glamorgan, was admitted to hospital nearly three weeks ago after becoming unwell while riding one of her horses.

After her partner proposed from her hospital bedside, staff on the Tegid Ward volunteered to pull together a celebration that included flowers, decorations, a harpist, food, cake and Heginbothom's beloved horses Ozzy and Quiosque.

The horses were brought to the hospital by Pen Llŷn Stud and Riding School, where Heginbothom rode and competed for many years.

"From the beautiful decorations to all the little touches that made our wedding so special, I cannot thank them enough," she said.

Ward manager Rachel Parry said her team were determined to get things right.

"On the morning of the wedding, we transformed Maggie's room with white sheets and fairy lights to create a beautiful space for the ceremony, while the relatives' room became a reception area," she said.

"Everything ran like clockwork, and some of our colleagues even came in on their days off to help make it happen.

"It was such a special and emotional occasion.

"There wasn't a dry eye in the room, and it was particularly lovely that some of the other patients Maggie has got to know during her time on the ward were able to join the celebrations."

Matron Ceri Newell said it was an example of the compassion and dedication shown by NHS staff.

"Nursing is about so much more than treating illness," she said.

"It is about compassion, kindness, humanity and recognising that sometimes the most important thing we can do is help make someone's wishes come true.

"What the team achieved for Maggie and Mark in such a short space of time was truly remarkable, and I could not be prouder of every single person involved.

"Everyone went above and beyond, working together to create something incredibly special for a couple going through such a difficult time.

"Moments like these remind us why we do what we do, and I am so proud of what the team achieved."

articles.title: Nvidia: How the Jensen Huang scandal exposed a headache for business-friendly Singapore
articles.summary: The scandal has cast a spotlight on Singapore's success as a chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
articles.body:
A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.

On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.

For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.

With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.

Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.

But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.

It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

The city-state has had some success in policing this.

It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.

They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.

In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.

The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.

Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.

But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.

Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.

In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.

Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.

Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.

In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.

Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.

Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.

On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".

China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.

How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.

In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.

For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.

But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.

Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.

BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.

In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.

Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.

During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.

Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.

Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.

All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore.

"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.

Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".

But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.

With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.

Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.

Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.

"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.

But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".

"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."

Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.
